target: कमल भाई, आपकी तबीयत कैसी है अब?
english: Kamal brother, how is your health now?
tip: भाई (bhai = brother) attaches to any man's name as friendly respect – कमल भाई (Kamal bhai) is not your sibling. Hindi lends family words to everyone.

target: कविता, ज़रा इधर तो आना।
english: Kavita, come over here for a sec.
tip: आना (aana) is just the base 'to come' form, used here as a soft, friendly request – 'do come over'. It lands gentler than the bare command आ (aa).

target: तू फ़िक्र मत कर, सब ठीक हो जाएगा।
english: Don't you worry, everything will be fine.
tip: तू (tu) is the most intimate of Hindi's three words for 'you' – close friends, kids, God. With a stranger it can insult. The safe default is आप (aap).

target: जी, मैं थोड़ी देर में आपको फ़ोन कर देता हूँ।
english: Sure, I'll call you back in a little while.
tip: जी (ji) alone at the start of a reply means 'yes' or 'sure' – the same syllable that adds respect after a name. One tiny word, two polite jobs.

target: तुलसीदास ने रामचरितमानस लिखी।
english: Tulsidas wrote Ramcharitmanas.
tip: With ने (ne), the verb agrees with what was written, not the writer: रामचरितमानस (Ramcharitmanas) is treated as feminine, so लिखी (likhi) – even though Tulsidas is a man.

target: विजय ने अपनी ज़िंदगी का एक बड़ा फ़ैसला लिया।
english: Vijay made a big decision in his life.
tip: English makes a decision; Hindi takes one: फ़ैसला लिया (faisla liya = took a decision), with लेना (lena = to take) as the partner verb.

target: कृपया आवेदन शुक्रवार तक जमा करें।
english: Please submit the application by Friday.
tip: तक (tak) covers both 'by' and 'until'. शुक्रवार तक (shukravaar tak) is a deadline here – by Friday – but with an ongoing action the same तक reads as until. Context decides.

target: जिसने भी यह फ़िल्म देखी, उसने तारीफ़ की।
english: Everyone who watched this film praised it.
tip: Hindi pairs its relatives: जिसने (jisne = whoever) must be answered by उसने (usne) in the second half. English drops the second pronoun – Hindi keeps both.

target: ज़िंदगी और जीवन दोनों एक ही बात है।
english: Zindagi and jeevan both mean the same thing.
tip: Hindi runs two word stocks side by side: ज़िंदगी (zindagi) is the Persian-side word, जीवन (jeevan) the Sanskrit-side one. Same meaning – zindagi sounds everyday, jeevan formal or literary.

target: अगर बारिश न होती तो फ़सल बर्बाद हो जाती।
english: If it hadn't rained, the crop would have been ruined.
tip: No 'would have' word here – the -ती (-ti) ending alone marks the unreal past: न होती... बर्बाद हो जाती (na hoti... barbaad ho jaati) = hadn't rained... would have been ruined.

target: रीता जितना सोचती है, उतना ही उलझती जाती है।
english: The more Rita thinks, the more confused she gets.
tip: 'The more... the more' is a matched pair in Hindi: जितना (jitna = as much) opens, उतना ही (utna hi = that much) closes. One without the other sounds unfinished.

target: थूककर चाटना उसकी आदत है, बात से मुकर जाता है।
english: Breaking his word is his habit; he goes back on his promises.
tip: थूककर चाटना (thook-kar chaatna) is literally 'to spit, then lick it back up' – Hindi's image for breaking your word: reclaiming something you already put out.

target: सूचित किया जाता है कि कार्यालय सोमवार को बंद रहेगा।
english: It is hereby notified that the office will remain closed on Monday.
tip: सूचित किया जाता है (soochit kiya jaata hai = it is informed) never names who is informing. This doer-less passive is the standard opener of official Hindi notices.

target: रंगमंच पर पर्दा उठते ही तालियाँ बजीं।
english: Applause rang out as the curtain rose on the stage.
tip: पर्दा उठते ही (parda uthte hi) = 'the instant the curtain rose'. Verb + ते ही (te hi) squeezes a whole 'as soon as' clause into the verb plus one tiny word.

target: कमल, मत जाओ ना, यहीं रुक जाओ।
english: Kamal, don't go, stay right here.
tip: The ना (na) after मत जाओ (mat jao = don't go) is not a 'no' – tacked onto a request it softens it, like 'come on, don't go'. मत (mat) alone does the forbidding.

target: यहाँ खाना बहुत अच्छा पकाया जाता है।
english: Food is cooked very well here.
tip: पकाया जाता है (pakaya jata hai = is cooked) is built on जाना (jaana = to go): literally 'goes cooked'. Hindi's passive runs on 'go', not on 'is' like English.

target: यात्रियों से अनुरोध है कि वे अपना सामान संभालकर रखें।
english: Passengers are requested to keep their belongings safe.
tip: यात्रियों से अनुरोध है (yatriyon se anurodh hai) is literally 'from passengers a request is' – Hindi requests point से (se = from) at the person being asked, not 'to' them.

target: टिकट बाबू ने खिड़की से टिकट काटा।
english: The ticket clerk punched the ticket from the window.
tip: टिकट काटा (tikat kaata) is literally 'cut a ticket' – काटना (kaatna = to cut) is the standard verb for issuing tickets, receipts, and fines, from tearing them off a pad.

target: इस होली पर आप हमारे घर अवश्य पधारें।
english: Do come to our home this Holi.
tip: पधारें (padharein) is an honorific 'come', used on invitations to mean 'grace us with a visit'. In everyday speech you would say आएँ (aayein) – पधारें signals ceremony.

target: इस दुख की घड़ी में हम आपके साथ हैं।
english: In this hour of grief, we are with you.
tip: घड़ी (ghadi) usually means watch or clock, but दुख की घड़ी (dukh ki ghadi) is 'hour of grief' – घड़ी also names a moment in time, like English 'hour' in 'darkest hour'.

target: कार्यालय त्योहार के कारण कल बंद रहेगा।
english: The office will remain closed tomorrow on account of the festival.
tip: बंद रहेगा (band rahega) is 'will stay closed', not 'will be closed' – for a state holding through the day, Hindi prefers रहना (rahna = to stay) over होना (hona = to be).

target: झूले पर बैठकर बच्चा आसमान छूना चाहता था।
english: Sitting on the swing, the child wanted to touch the sky.
tip: बैठकर (baithkar) = 'having sat' – where English says 'sitting on the swing', Hindi adds -कर (kar) to the first action: sit-then-want, all in one word.

target: देखा जा सकता है कि पिछले दशक में बहुत बदलाव आया है।
english: It can be seen that a lot of change has come in the last decade.
tip: देखा जा सकता है (dekha ja sakta hai) = 'it can be seen' – literally 'seen go can'. Hindi builds 'can be X-ed' with जाना (jana = go) after the main verb.

target: वकालतनामे पर हस्ताक्षर करवाए गए।
english: Signatures were obtained on the power of attorney document.
tip: करवाए गए (karvaye gaye) = 'were gotten done' – the -वा- (va) inside the verb means someone else did it. करना (karna) = do, करवाना (karvana) = have someone do.

target: सभी कर्मचारियों से अनुरोध है कि वे अपनी रिपोर्ट शुक्रवार तक जमा करें।
english: All employees are requested to submit their reports by Friday.
tip: Requests come FROM people in Hindi: कर्मचारियों से अनुरोध है (karmchariyon se anurodh hai) = 'from the employees is a request' – से (se = from), not 'to'.

target: त्योहार के कारण कार्यालय सोमवार को बंद रहेगा।
english: The office will remain closed on Monday on account of the festival.
tip: 'Because of' follows its noun: त्योहार के कारण (tyohar ke kaaran) = 'festival because-of'. के कारण (ke kaaran) always comes after the reason, never before.

target: उम्मीद है कि परिणाम अगले सप्ताह घोषित किए जाएँगे।
english: It is expected that the results will be announced next week.
tip: English needs 'It is expected that' – Hindi just says उम्मीद है कि (ummeed hai ki = hope is that). No dummy 'it': the noun उम्मीद (ummeed = hope) leads.

target: चोर की दाढ़ी में तिनका देखकर पकड़ लिया।
english: They caught the thief by spotting a straw in his beard.
tip: चोर की दाढ़ी में तिनका (chor ki daadhi mein tinka) = 'a straw in the thief's beard' – guilt betrays itself. The nervous thief checks his own beard first.

target: बिल्ली चुपके से दूध पी गई।
english: The cat quietly drank the milk.
tip: पी गई (pee gayi) is drink + go, but the cat didn't go anywhere – the added 'go' marks the milk as completely finished. Hindi pairs verbs like this to show an action is done.

target: जिसकी लाठी उसकी भैंस, ताक़तवर जीतता है।
english: Might is right–the powerful wins.
tip: जिसकी लाठी उसकी भैंस (jiski laathi uski bhains) is literally 'whose stick, his buffalo' – whoever holds the stick keeps the buffalo. That is Hindi's image for might is right.
